Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Hello everyone, and thank you for joining Adyen's H1 2026 earnings call. My name is Maggie O'Donnell from Investor Relations, and I will be hosting today's call. With me today are Pieter, our co-founder and co-CEO, and Hwa, our incoming Interim CFO. We are going to begin with playing the prepared remarks from Ingo and Hwa, then Pieter will say a few words, and finally, we will open it up for Q&A with Pieter and Hwa. If you would like to ask a question, please use the raise hand functionality at the bottom of your screen. With that, let us get started.

Ingo Uytdehaage (Co-CEO, Adyen): Hello, everyone. The beginning of 2026 was a strategically important half for Adyen. As commerce rapidly evolves, we are enabling more of the world's largest merchants to capture greater value across the entire commerce journey. We grow faster than our market. This consistent outperformance is driven by two engines. First, we are winning new and diverse customers. Second, we are deepening relationships and expanding our share of wallet with existing ones. Both reflect our ability to continuously deliver new value for our customers. Our long-term relationships provide clear visibility into the durability of this growth. Merchants typically expand their share of wallet with Adyen from under 20% in years three to seven, to more than 40% after year 12. Even after more than a decade, customers like Uber, Microsoft, Spotify, and Google continue to broaden their use of our platform.
This sustained expansion gives us ultimate confidence in our resilience and ability to continue outperforming the market. The strong momentum reflected in our H1 performance comes from our unchanged mission, solving complexity for our merchants. The complexity is only increasing as commerce rapidly evolves. Competition for consumer attention is fiercer than ever. Workflows are shifting rapidly to AI, and legacy infrastructure is no longer sufficient to meet the demands of modern digital commerce. Our long-term strategy is built for exactly this shift, which is why more customers are looking to us as a stronger partner. Our North Star is to become the single trusted platform for the financial infrastructure on which global commerce runs. We started by building the world's most advanced payments processing stack. Now we are expanding that same engineering first mindset to solve customer pain points before at and after the transaction.
Our payments engine remains our foundation, and it continues to win share, but we are no longer just a payments company. We are the complete financial operating system for modern commerce, from payments to loyalty, billing, and Intelligent Money Movement. You can see this focus in high impact milestones we delivered this half. First, we completed the acquisitions of Talon.One and Orb, moving us deeper into our customers' technology stack and extending our platform well beyond payments. Talon.One brings market-leading promotions and loyalty capabilities into our single platform. Combined with our unique online and in-person transaction data, it allows merchants to finally deliver truly omnichannel loyalty at scale. For years, retailers have struggled to connect digital and physical customer experiences.
By bringing loyalty natively into our architecture, merchants can recognize shoppers across channels and deliver personalized incentives in real time, deepening consumer engagement and making loyalty far more effective than standalone systems ever could. Orb addresses another growing customer challenge. As AI transforms how software is built and consumed, usage-based billing is becoming the default pricing model for many businesses. Orb gives merchants the tools to automate metering, pricing, and billing, while our payment infrastructure completes the revenue life cycle by connecting usage directly to settlement. Together, this gives businesses a single system to launch flexible pricing models globally and at scale. These acquisitions are an important part of our long-term strategy, serving as powerful drivers of our growth. They represent our fundamental long-term belief that in a complex world, the company that facilitates revenue optimization will deliver the most value.
It also reflects how we invest, selectively, with discipline, and where we see clear strategic logic. Second, we introduced Adyen Agentic to solve a critical problem for our merchants, how to sell safely and efficiently in the emerging AI agent economy. Without a universal standard, merchants would need to build and maintain dozens of separate integrations just to keep their inventory, pricing, and payments in sync. This creates massive operational cost and risk. Our product suite solves this. It acts as the universal translator that allows merchants to connect once to our platform and securely accept payments across all major Agentic protocols, all while using the same unified fraud detection and compliance rules they trust today. Third, we officially launched Intelligent Money Movement. For large enterprise merchants, complexity doesn't end at a point of payment — i t often begins there.
We help businesses automate global money movement on a single unified platform. Because this occurs natively on our own technical and banking infrastructure, capital flows dynamically and without the frictional delays of traditional banking rails. It allows us to move money completely end to end, unlocking unprecedented speed and treasury efficiency, so global businesses can simplify their most complex operations. Taken together, these capabilities make Adyen a more strategic partner to our customers and strengthen our long-term growth opportunity. The success of this strategy is directly reflected in our financial results this half. We delivered a strong half of 2026, with net revenue up 21% on a constant currency basis, driven by this ongoing platform expansion. Our scale is already immense. We are processing billions of transactions for thousands of global merchants. In the first half alone, we processed EUR 804 billion in volume.
To reiterate, we are winning in the market because we are building the complete financial operating system for modern commerce. As we look to the second half of 2026 and beyond, we will continue to execute with the same speed, discipline, and engineering-first mindset that has brought us here. We hold ourselves to the same standard with you, our shareholders, setting clear commitments and delivering against them consistently. To speak more to our operation execution and financial performance, I'll now hand things over to our interim CFO, Hwa Tsao. Hwa, over to you.

Hwa Tsao (Interim CFO, Adyen): Hello, everyone. I am Hwa Tsao, Adyen's incoming interim CFO. For the past year, I have worked alongside the management board as the SVP of Group Finance, and I am thrilled to step into this role at such a strategically important time for Adyen, marked by our recent acquisitions of Talon.One and Orb, the launch of Intelligent Money Movement and Adyen Agentic, and so much more. My focus is on empowering our incredible team to serve our customers and continuing our history of financial discipline while keeping our dialogue with our investors transparent and constructive. Now, let us turn to our financials, beginning with our top-line results. Net revenue was EUR 1.3 billion in the first half, up 19% year-over-year or 21% on a constant currency basis, with continued strong growth in line with our communicated guidance. The best way to understand Adyen's net revenue growth is through our building blocks.
First, expanding share of wallet with existing customers. Second, ramping up previous year cohorts. Third, winning new merchants, and fourth, scaling our financial products. We drove roughly two-thirds of our growth by deepening relationships with our existing merchants, specifically those onboarded before 2025. As Ingo highlighted, compounding revenue from established merchant cohorts is a valuable driver of our business. When our merchants expand, we grow with them. In addition, as we help them solve more challenges across products and geographies, we increase our share of their wallet. These levers, combined with volume-based tiered pricing, incentivize our merchants to consolidate more of their business onto our platform as they scale. The remainder of our growth came from the ramp of our 2025 cohort, new customer wins in 2026, and the expansion of our financial products offering.
These levers lay the foundation for the future as more recent wins scale and drive our continued growth for years to come. To support this expanding business, we added 249 net new joiners in the first half, bringing our total FTEs to 5,020 at the end of June. Our disciplined and targeted approach to hiring focused primarily on technical and go-to-market roles to drive our product roadmap and commercial momentum. With this focus, we remain well on track for our full-year goal of 550 to 650 net new hires. This measured pace of investment directly supported our strong profitability. EBITDA reached EUR 642 million for the first half, up 18% year-over-year for an EBITDA margin of 49%. Excluding one-time transaction costs, EBITDA margin landed at 50%, in line with H1 2025 and our previously communicated expectations.
CapEx was EUR 64 million or 5% of net revenue in the first half. The majority of our CapEx is related to data centers. Our core infrastructure operates on our own private cloud, which creates a commercial advantage and allows us to deliver operational efficiency as we scale. Now, I would like to say a few words on our approach to capital allocation. We are in a high-growth phase, and sustained efficient growth is our single highest priority. Everything we have done and everything we will do demonstrates this commitment. We put our capital to work where it drives the greatest long-term value. In the first half of 2026, our strong balance sheet allowed us to invest in our team to drive innovation, strengthen our platform infrastructure to support global scale, and execute targeted M&A to accelerate our roadmap and reach, as you saw with Talon.One and Orb.
Looking ahead, we remain fully focused on capturing the massive opportunity in front of us. Moving on to our outlook for the rest of the year. For net revenues, we now expect full year 2026 net revenue growth of 21%-23% year-over-year on a constant currency basis. This reflects a 1 percentage point contribution from the acquisitions for the full year, or 2 percentage points of contribution in the second half. Our growth outlook for the underlying organic business is unchanged, and we expect the growth rate in the second half to be similar to the first half, excluding the impact of Talon.One and Orb. On EBITDA, we expect our underlying 2026 EBITDA margin to remain in line with 2025. Including the two acquisitions, we expect a 1 percentage point dilution, leading full year EBITDA margin to land approximately 1% point lower than 2025.
We remain on track to achieve our 2028 objective of an EBITDA margin above 55%. Finally, CapEx. Data center infrastructure that supports the growth of our platform accounts for the majority of our CapEx spend. We are proactively pulling investment from 2027 into H2 2026 to secure compute and storage availability and lock in price amid an unprecedented demand environment. As a result, we now expect CapEx of approximately 7% of net revenue for the full year. Through this active management, we expect CapEx to return towards historical levels post 2026. In summary, we delivered a strong first half with 21% constant currency revenue growth and 50% underlying EBITDA margins. We continue to deepen our relationships with our existing merchants like Toast and win new customers like OpenAI, while expanding our platform through new product offerings and strategic acquisitions like Talon.One and Orb.
We enter the second half of 2026 with high confidence in our position and our ability to capture the massive opportunity ahead.

Pieter van der Does (Co-Founder and Co-CEO, Adyen): Thanks, everybody, for joining us today. I want to add a few words to what Ingo and Hwa just said. When I started out Adyen 20 years ago, the mission was simple: solve real complexity for our merchants. Twenty years later, we are still doing exactly that, and we are really good at it. Back then, merchant pain points were mostly around checkout. Today, global enterprises face challenges across their total financial operations, so we evolved. We didn't just build a payment engine, we built a platform that powers modern commerce end to end, from customer loyalty to complex money movement. We went beyond payments. Recently, we marked an exciting milestone with two acquisitions. What's most important is that our identity hasn't changed. We have always evolved with our merchants' needs. We build great technology, eliminate friction, and stay laser focused on what our merchants need.
The positive response from those merchants to this direction, including the acquisitions, reinforces that we are the strategic partner they look for solving their most complex challenges. This is key to our success, and H1 has been another very positive half, and I'm excited for what's to come. Looking forward to answering your questions and I'll hand it over to you, Maggie.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Thank you, Pieter. We're going to move on to Q&A now. As a reminder, if you have a question, please use the raise hand functionality at the bottom of your screen. When we call on you, please unmute your microphone before asking your question. Our first question comes from Andrew Schmidt at KeyBanc. Andrew, please go ahead and unmute yourself and ask your question.

Andrew Schmidt (Analyst, KeyBanc): Thank you very much. Hi, Pieter. Hi, Hwa. Thank you for taking the question. Maybe just on the platform evolution. Clearly a lot of significant progress over the last six to 12 months towards this new financial operating system model. Maybe talk a little bit about what catalyzed the change. When we think about further areas of expansion, some examples of places you go, there's clearly a lot of opportunity. Just one additional one if I could squeeze in. As the platform expands, you have more opportunities to go after new clients and existing client expansion with the new capabilities. Maybe just talk about how the visibility of the business evolves as well. Thank you so much.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Thanks, Andrew. I think Pieter, you can take both of those questions.

Pieter van der Does (Co-Founder and Co-CEO, Adyen): All right. If you look at our platform evolution, we started 20 years ago with being very good at processing payments online. Each so many years, we have added a lot of functionality. If you look at that journey, which I see as a continuum, it brought us to where we are today. In that expansion and looking at what our merchants need, you see that AI puts new challenges on them, which is for SaaS platform, metered billing, which is for merchants, how do I really cement my relationship with shoppers? That brings loyalty top on the agenda. Our latest additions to the platform, Intelligent Money Movement, we have been working on that for longer. I look at it as a continuum.
Well, there's newish that we did through acquisitions, but there's nothing new in the sense that we always evolve with our merchants.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): The second question on visibility into future areas of growth with customers.

Pieter van der Does (Co-Founder and Co-CEO, Adyen): As I talk about how we are very close to our merchants, how we partner with our merchants, we are in close contact. Our existing merchants continue to grow with us. New merchants are at the beginning of the journey. That means that we don't have a roadmap for the next five years. It's that we stay agile and that we will develop everything what they need to take complexity around the payment away from them.

Hwa Tsao (Interim CFO, Adyen): In the near term, I will also add just for Talon.One And Orb, both of those have been extremely well-received by our customer base. Pieter, I know his phone has been ringing off the hook, with some of the use cases we talked about, as well as new ones that maybe we did not even consider while we were going down that path. There is a lot of opportunity even in the near term with these new capabilities.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Great. Thank you so much for your questions, Andrew. The next question comes from Harshita Rawat from Bernstein. Harshita, please go ahead and unmute yourself and ask your question.

Harshita Rawat (Analyst, Bernstein): Hi. Good morning. Hwa, can you maybe talk about your revenue growth targets? I know the organic constant currency number is essentially the same. The second quarter was very strong. Looking into the second half, you have new client wins ramping up, you have benefit from strong 2025 cohorts. How should we think about the likelihood of you coming in at different points of the range and also any comments on Q3 versus 4Q? Pieter, it is very early days, but as you just closed the Talon.One and Orb acquisitions, maybe talk about what you are hearing from customers with respect to demand for loyalty, usage-based billing, and also how is the integration going from a cultural point of view? Thank you.

Hwa Tsao (Interim CFO, Adyen): Thanks, Harshita. On the second half as you said, our first half was a strong one. We landed right in the middle of the guide for the year at 21%. As we stated before, we do expect performance to be similar. We continue to grow with our existing customers and add new wins along the way, and those dynamics we expect to continue as we go forward. The thing I will call out, the only real change as you mentioned, is for the impact of the acquisitions. Those you will see impacting the second half as we push forward.

Pieter van der Does (Co-Founder and Co-CEO, Adyen): Yeah. The customer demand for those services. I have been speaking to merchants this week. What is top of mind for them is, "How do I make sure that in an age of AI, I do not see a disintermediation?" Loyalty is top of mind for them. I actually happened to also speak to a couple of merchants who were already on Talon.One and Adyen and who are really thrilled that now the services will be used together. AI on data is very strong, but the data is very important to have. Now with Orb, with Talon.One and with Adyen, the data set is just more sophisticated, so there is more we can do, and that is what they really appreciate. Orb, if you look at AI native, that is billing and you see that opens up a market for us where we can land very mature companies.
If you look at a company like OpenAI working for us, that is just for payments. That is for payments of their consumers. But together with Orb, that also opens up the avenue to pick up more AI native companies earlier in their journey.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): The point on the integration of how the integration is going so far.

Pieter van der Does (Co-Founder and Co-CEO, Adyen): I do not underestimate integrations. I have sold a company to Worldpay. It was a very successful integration, but there were also lessons learned. When we looked at the integration, we bought companies which are culturally aligned and which are in geographies close to our offices. Still, what I think makes this integration easier is that this is an integration done for growth. There are exciting integrations also for the companies. It is not about cost cutting, it is about making those products work together. That is what we are currently doing. We are actually slightly ahead of plan there, and there is a lot of excitement around it.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Great. Thank you for your question, Harshita. The next question comes from Hannes Leitner from Jefferies. Hannes, please go ahead and unmute yourself and ask your question.

Hannes Leitner (Analyst, Jefferies): Yes, thanks for letting me on. I got also a couple of questions. Maybe the first one is just like a high level. You talked about or you dropped a lot of outstanding merchant wins and very fast ramp-ups. Maybe you can talk about kind of how is the playing field changing? Has this revisiting of contracts and expansion of contracts, the time shortened and you are clearly now able to scale much more? So a philosophical question to you, Pieter. Then maybe just like one other thing is, I remember very well you mentioned when you launched embedded finance product a couple of years or when you announced it, one of the items was that you will use your balance sheet. It hasn't really come through that you have scaled loans and financing.
Yes, we understand that some of that hasn't really hit the let's say, the threshold that you unleashed the rail guards. Maybe you can talk about that, what data points you expect to see, and how does this tie in to wins like the last platform win, with the expansion with Toast, for example. Is that a customer to target there in the long term? Thank you.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Thanks, Hannes. Pieter, why don't you take the question on the landscape and then touch on embedded financial products and Hwa can end that question.

Pieter van der Does (Co-Founder and Co-CEO, Adyen): I think if you look at the landscape, there is no other company that can do everything that Adyen can do. For large merchants, it is logical to move to us, and I think that that position for us only gets stronger. That is something what we see and continuously see. If I move on to the question which, for example, you mentioned Toast, without talking about the services to an individual merchant, I can give some voiceover. What you see there, that is a merchant which has already been working for us for a longer time and is now ramping up and giving us more share of market. That is a pattern that we typically see.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): On embedded financial products in general, how is that going?

Pieter van der Does (Co-Founder and Co-CEO, Adyen): Embedded financial products, they add about 1% contribution to this year. It is an important service for us because in the choice for a platform to work with us, they want to know that they can also do those services with us. They do not always take them from the beginning, and the reason why we less talk about it this time is because there is so much to talk about it, so there is a wealth of information to share.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Okay, great. The next question comes from Adam Frisch at Evercore. Adam, please go ahead and unmute yourself and ask your question.

Adam Frisch (Analyst, Evercore): Okay, thanks, and good morning. Two questions for you. How does the pipeline look in terms of new merchant wins coming online, and how does that bode for near-term growth rates? The second question is, with regard to the cash on your balance sheet, great call-out on the shareholder letter that there's a little under EUR 5 billion ex the merchant liabilities, et cetera. How much of that is needed for reserves for banking licenses, and how much is available to deploy in areas like M&A or if you do a buyback and stuff like that? Thank you.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Pieter, do you want to start?

Pieter van der Does (Co-Founder and Co-CEO, Adyen): Yeah. If you look at what is happening in our pipeline, Adyen is sort of a boring machine. We are constantly signing up new merchants, bringing them to life, getting some share of wallet and over time, you see that we grow, and that growth process takes on for years and years and years. That engine is just running like it always was, so there's no deviation from earlier years.

Hwa Tsao (Interim CFO, Adyen): On the point about the actual cash, the reality is we don't just need it for regulatory reserves. We also have operational buffers. We keep a fair amount of cash on our balance sheet for credit ratings purposes and ultimately, it also helps us fuel our growth. So we won't give an exact number, but I think the reality is the number that you see on the financials, the available cash or the excess cash is a small fraction of that amount.

Pieter van der Does (Co-Founder and Co-CEO, Adyen): If I can add something to that. The reality is that it's a fraction of a number that I've seen flying around. If I look at the business, there is so much room for growth that we have a focus on building that growth, and that's the way how we create value. I'm way more interested in that, and we need to have some room and you see that we used that room this year. We've never been dogmatic about that. It just happened to fall this year. We want to have an open mind in the future and think about what's the best way to grow this business continuously at a high rate.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Great. Thank you for your questions, Adam Frisch. The next question comes from Darrin Peller from Wolfe. Darrin, please go ahead and ask your question.

Darrin Peller (Analyst, Wolfe): Thanks. Let me just start off, on, with a macro question, and then I just want to ask Hwa Tsao a quick margin question. On the macro side, if you could just discuss what you're seeing in EMEA year-to-date, spending patterns, especially amidst the Middle East conflict, and then travel trends as well. If you can give any color on what you're seeing even quarter-to-date through mid-August, that'd be really helpful. Then just on the margin side, maybe just reiterate what gives you the conviction in reaching the 55% + EBITDA margins by 2028. Just what are the key levers to get there? Thanks again, guys.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Pieter, do you want to take both of those?

Pieter van der Does (Co-Founder and Co-CEO, Adyen): All right. If you see what's happening in spending patterns. For us, we have less detail than you would think because we grow about three times what the market grows. That means that all our numbers are also a little bit changed because we get more share of wallet. Currently, we can absorb in our number the trends. If you look at why would we say 55%, that number I describe the business. If you grow the top line, then you know that you will get to a higher EBITDA. That is why we grow to that number. Rather than a target, it is an outcome.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Okay, great. Thanks for your questions. The next question comes from Sanjay Sakhrani from KBW. Please go ahead and ask your question.

Sanjay Sakhrani (Analyst, KBW): Thank you. Good morning. I guess, Pieter, maybe you could talk a little bit about the OpenAI win. Obviously, it is a meaningful win. Some of your competitors have had some success in AI, a little bit more than Adyen. I am curious what the sales cycle was and what might be the nature of that relationship, and then what the pipeline looks like for more in this space. Secondly, just Hwa, if you don't mind expanding a little bit on the CapEx commentary as we look to next year. I know you said it should normalize. Do you anticipate any additional pressure from some of the higher costs, or can we even see a CapEx level that is lower next year as a result of this pull forward? Thank you.

Pieter van der Does (Co-Founder and Co-CEO, Adyen): All right. I think it is good to point out on the OpenAI relationship that we work with them as an LLM, as we do with all the parties. That is to help our merchants. This is something else. This is to provide payments to them. I don't talk that much about individual customers. What you see, it is a trend that the largest companies like to partner with Adyen. I think that is a trend that you consistently see, and it is there to continue.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Yeah, to be super clear it is an Adyen Agentic partner and also a customer. There are two parts to this relationship. Hwa, on CapEx?

Hwa Tsao (Interim CFO, Adyen): Yeah. On CapEx, what you saw in our increased guidance for this year is a deliberate decision. We are pulling forward the spend. We are not going to provide an outlook right now for 2027. We will do that at the beginning of next year. But obviously, we are actively managing this, and we will take opportunities. What you saw ultimately was we saw the opportunity to secure supply at a good price and we took it, and you will see us actively manage CapEx in the future.

Pieter van der Does (Co-Founder and Co-CEO, Adyen): To add to that, it is not the first time we are doing that. We did it during COVID as well in 2022, where we thought smart buying is the way to deal with the market dynamics. Also then you saw that after that, CapEx returned to historical levels.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Okay, great. Thank you for your questions. The next question comes from Pavan Daswani from Citi. Pavan, please go ahead and unmute yourself and ask your question.

Pavan Daswani (Analyst, Citi): Thanks, Maggie. Hi, Pieter and Hwa. Thanks for taking my questions. Maybe firstly on Intelligent Money Movement, could you touch on any learnings from early customer deployments? Stepping back, was the strategic ambition primarily solving a merchant treasury and liquidity problem, or was it expanding Adyen's role beyond payment acceptance and into broader money infrastructure? Secondly, a higher level one. Historically, Adyen has always been seen as a payments company, but with embedded finance, Intelligent Money Movement, and acquisitions such as Orb and Talon.One, you are increasingly moving to multiple layers of the commerce stack. Maybe looking out five years from now, should we still think of Adyen primarily as a payments company or a broader commerce infrastructure platform?

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Great questions. Thank you. Do you want to actually start with the second question and then go to IMM after?

Pieter van der Does (Co-Founder and Co-CEO, Adyen): Let us look philosophically at what Adyen does. What we do is we do the transaction, and we do everything around it which is adjacent. We serve the merchant. That is who we are selling to, and all the complexity around the payment is for us, quite a large area. Because of our banking licenses in multiple geographies, because of how we are regulated, we can take a lot out of their hands. For example, if we see that money will come in, we can already provide that liquidity, but that is something for which you need a banking license. More philosophically, do you see other services coming up? Yes, everything that is around the transaction, but it will always be close to the transaction. I do not see unrelated services coming into scope very quickly.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): On IMM, any early learnings from rolling this out with our customers?

Pieter van der Does (Co-Founder and Co-CEO, Adyen): There's an enormous need for it, and we have so much data around it that we are very well positioned. These are further avenues for growth for the future, and we have so many of them that I'm quite excited about the position we're in.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Great. Thank you for your questions. The next question comes from Justin Forsythe from UBS. Justin, please go ahead and unmute yourself and ask your question.

Justin Forsythe (Analyst, UBS): Hey, good afternoon. Pieter, welcome back to the hot seat, and Hwa, welcome as well. Thanks, Maggie. Couple questions from my end. First, I wanted to hone in a little bit on Orb and the meter billing opportunity. Maybe you can talk about how it helps your go-to-market motion with SaaS platforms and AI companies, and how important it is to buy rather than partner billing platforms as you had done in the past. Further, how important is it to have an established brand and go to market such as Orb, to sell to native AI companies versus building it from scratch? Pieter, if I'm not mistaken, this is something maybe you've considered doing internally, building a billing function. Why did you decide to not at that point in time, and why yes now to owning it?
Hwa, a financial question for you, maybe asked in a slightly different way, which is I think, we said around the 1Q that 1Q would be the slowest growth of the year. Is that something that we can reconfirm on an organic ex-FX basis? I guess that comment is mostly directed at the 3Q, but in general.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): I think we might have accidentally muted you, Justin. I am so sorry. We can answer the first couple of questions. Do you want to take the one on Orb first, Pieter?

Pieter van der Does (Co-Founder and Co-CEO, Adyen): How does Orb help us? You see that SaaS platforms become metered billing, so that is an opportunity for us to help them there. It helps us with native AI companies, you see that there is so much pressure on them that all the resource goes to developing their product. So to combine billing and payments there is quite a logical step. This opens up a part of the market for us, which is less logical to buy elements independently from each other. What we have done when we considered how to go about with billing, don't forget that Adyen of course, we build billing because we bill our own merchants. So that was one avenue we looked at. Are we going to expand our own billing service to something? We were already partnering, and we also looked at acquiring.
We also considered you could also say, let's not build this service. I do not think that was the best option. Whereas we usually land on building it ourselves, it just happened that this time we felt that it was better to use a resource somewhere else, and it was better to deploy our capital here to acquire it, shorter time to market and more focus on our other products. On the other hand, I do not underestimate integrations, but the products fit very well together. They are in San Francisco in our office, so there are a lot of things going forward for it, why we decided to go differently this time.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Hwa on the quarter?

Hwa Tsao (Interim CFO, Adyen): Justin, we do not manage the business on a quarter to quarter. We have provided a full year guide, and frankly, the business can be a little bit lumpy. What we said, and I will reiterate, is that we do expect the second half to be similar to the first half in terms of growth on an underlying basis. And we will see the impact of Talon.One and Orb as well.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Thanks for your questions, Justin, and you can email us that last question that we cut off. Sorry about that. The next question comes from Rayna Kumar from OpCo. Rayna, please go ahead and unmute yourself and ask your question.

Rayna Kumar (Analyst, OpCo): Competitive pricing, like has pricing intensified over the last six months? Thank you.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): All right. You were cut off at the beginning. I am not sure what is going on. If you do not mind repeating that would be very helpful.

Rayna Kumar (Analyst, OpCo): Could you comment on competitive pricing? Has it intensified over the last six months? Thank you.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Thank you. Pieter, do you want to take that one?

Pieter van der Does (Co-Founder and Co-CEO, Adyen): Yes, happy to take that question. I think that we have seen competition all over, all the time, sometimes a bit more in one region than the other. But if you look at our data, you don't see it back in our data. Our existing merchants give us more and more volume and therefore come to lower tiers, and that's the only explanation behind the take rate developments. It's, for us, basically business as usual.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Okay, great. Thank you for your question. The next question comes from Fahed Kunwar from Rothschild & Co Redburn. Fahed, please go ahead and ask your question.

Fahed Kunwar (Analyst, Rothschild & Co Redburn): Cheers, Maggie, and thanks for taking the question, both. My question was actually about, just following up on the last question on EMEA and the U.S. digital net revenue growth. If I look at EMEA, the net revenue growth has slowed down. We were doing 26 a year and a bit ago, and now we're doing 15. I think, obviously in the U.S., we've had very strong growth. Just to get a sense of what's happening there is it the same merchants maybe shifting some volume from Europe to the U.S.? Is digital net revenues or is the U.S. revenues growing because you're winning share there and perhaps losing some share of wallet in Europe? Is there something else that we don't understand? Also thinking about that EMEA growth trend, where do you think that stabilizes? Any update on that would be great. Thank you.

Hwa Tsao (Interim CFO, Adyen): I'll try to take the first question. In terms of the regional mix, I think you did identify something, which is the fact that we work with global merchants. Some of them are based in EMEA, and they do shift, and they sell into other markets. Similarly, U.S. markets, U.S. based merchants will sell into other markets, and that's true for frankly, all of our global merchants because we manage our customers more on a customer basis as opposed to a territory-wide basis. I do think U.S. strength also does reflect the fact that we have been investing in the U.S. specifically. You saw that over the last few years, and so those investments are coming to bear fruit today. As far as EMEA, we don't really look at it from a stabilization perspective because it is a huge growth opportunity for us.
We've been performing very well, and as I said, we work with Europe-based merchants, and we sell around the world.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Great. Thank you, Hwa. The next question comes from Jason Kupferberg from Wells Fargo. Jason, please go ahead and ask your question.

Jason Kupferberg (Analyst, Wells Fargo): Thank you, guys. I wanted to go deeper into some of the wallet share gains. I feel like that was a big theme in the shareholder letter, and it is the single biggest building block, obviously, in your medium-term guidance. I am wondering if these share gains have been increasingly concentrated in a certain region, or are they more balanced across geographies, and are there any pockets of the business where you actually think that your share gains are accelerating, maybe due to Dynamic Identification or other drivers? My follow-up is on Adyen Agentic and just what has merchant receptiveness looked like so far, and any material amount of revenue yet? Thanks.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Hwa, do you want to take that first one?

Hwa Tsao (Interim CFO, Adyen): Yeah

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): He will do the second.

Hwa Tsao (Interim CFO, Adyen): On the wallet share gains, I think the reality is that we have a very diversified base of customers. We mentioned that the top 300 make up 60% of revenue, and we are seeing wallet share gains across all of them. I would not point to any specific region because we see strength. Obviously, some are more mature than others, but over time, we do have broad-based growth, and we expect that to continue. Pieter on the Adyen Agentic.

Pieter van der Does (Co-Founder and Co-CEO, Adyen): On the Agentic, we launched a number of things to help merchants to publish on the LLMs, which is in a way similar to payment methods. We have always been very good to connecting the merchants to multiple payment methods and taking complexity out. Now we have the possibility to help merchants with publishing on multiple Agentic protocols and take the complexity out, then after the transaction, bring it back into their environment so that all their existing functionality works. We went live with a number of merchants, as you saw in the shareholder letter. I will point out Sézane, a predominantly online French fashion brand that was very early with us doing that. There is a lot of talk about machine to machine. We are also heavily investing in that.
Do not forget that we service large merchants, and they also need a little bit guidance of us from what is there, what is real, and what we provide now. Therefore in the letter, we provide what we do now, but we are also ready for what will be happening a little bit later down the road.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): All right. Great. Thanks for your questions. The next question comes from Sandeep from JP Morgan. Sandeep, please go ahead and ask your question.

Speaker 16: Yeah, hi. Thanks for letting me on. My first question is regarding your two acquisitions, Talon.One and Orb. Historically, when Adyen releases new products, you have three to five customers that you trial the product with for quite a long time, after which you roll it out to the entire customer base. Is this the sort of strategy that you are adopting with these acquisitions regarding your existing customer base, where you will try to cross-sell those products into, or is there some different kind of strategy being adopted here? Associated with that, do you have some lead customers who are going to be using that? Secondly, my second question is regarding some of your older new products, such as issuing, where we are on issuing at this point, and how that is contributing to your revenue at this point. Thank you.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Pieter, do you want to take the first one on go-to-market for the acquisitions? Hwa, maybe you can comment on financial products.

Pieter van der Does (Co-Founder and Co-CEO, Adyen): When we announced the acquisition, there were more questions coming out of the woodworks than we anticipated. Why? That is because merchants are actively thinking about, "What is my strategy when I'll be faced with more Adyen Agentic?" It's top of mind for them, "How do I make sure that I have the whole infrastructure in place to get as much traffic as I can directly?" How do I pull my merchant in? We've been speaking about merchants doing both online and in store. They've been using their resource somewhere else, then connecting that and the insights. It's all about the data, having all the data together, of loyalty, of payments, of billing, and on that you can develop such strong products that that's what excites our merchants.
I've been speaking to merchants which wanted to get it and didn't have it, but also the last two merchants that I spoke to happened to be merchants which were already using both Talon.One and Adyen. We don't need to be tiptoeing around. This is a proven combination that works. But what we're doing is we're deepening the integration to make it more powerful. It's a growth acquisition. It's not an acquisition for cost-cutting in those companies.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Hwa, on the issuing and financial products contribution.

Hwa Tsao (Interim CFO, Adyen): Yeah. What I can say about issuing is we continue to see strong traction there. We are not going to break out specifics, but financial products as we stated, we continue to expect it to add about a point of growth this year, and it remains really important for all of our customer segments.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Perfect. Thank you so much. The next question comes from Bryan Bergin at TD Cowen. Bryan, please go ahead and ask your question.

Bryan Bergin (Analyst, TD Cowen): Hi. Thank you. My first question is on customer penetration. So appreciate the disclosure on the customer share of wallet as far as merchants often increasing from less than 20% in years three to seven to more than 40% after 12 years. Can you frame where the current customer base sits along that maturity curve as far as the rough mix of processing volume that comes from customers that have already reached the 40%+ share versus those that are in the earlier phases of penetration? My follow-up question is on AI investment and usage. Understanding the increased CapEx for data in infra here is being pulled forward, but from an OpEx standpoint, can you comment on how AI is impacting your cost structure? Just speak to how AI usage may be contributing to your 55%+ EBITDA margin target by 2028. Thank you.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Why don't we start on that second question, if you don't mind. Pieter, do you want to take that one?

Pieter van der Does (Co-Founder and Co-CEO, Adyen): Yeah. The operational cost, the OpEx one, it is because we saw an opportunity to lock in cost and supply. It is not related to that our data usage is suddenly different or our storage usage is suddenly different than it used to be in the past. It is the same typical compute and storage that we have, which grows with the business. As it grows with the business, remember, we are on private cloud, so we have our own data centers. At least we are in co-locations, but we are very happy with the choice. It is extremely efficient, more efficient than what our competitors run on. We see that it resonates with merchants. There are merchants who prefer to be on a company which is independent.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): I think

Hwa Tsao (Interim CFO, Adyen): Just a little more color on OpEx specifically. It is baked in. We are investing in AI tools. I think that might be another angle to the question. That is baked into our overall guidance that we have already put forward. I think on the customer penetration point, I guess I will start and then Pieter you can jump in. We have a really diversified base of customers. We have many merchants who have been with us for a long time, and we continue to add new cohorts along the way. So we are seeing concentration decline overall, and we do see significant room for expansion across the customer base with existing customers and new customers.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Perfect. Thank you for your questions. The next question comes from Fred Boulon at Bank of America. Fred, please go ahead and ask your question.

Fred Boulon (Analyst, Bank of America): Hey, thanks a lot for taking the question. Sorry, one second. Yeah, thanks a lot for taking the question. So two, please, two follow-up. One is on the prior question on opportunities ahead. Where do you see the most exciting opportunities, or how do you define areas where you can remove complexity for your merchants as you discussed earlier? Second, if you can come back on your capital allocation framework. As you state, you have over EUR 4 billion in net cash available post M&A, but only a fraction is really available. On a multi-year view, absent significant M&A, could we see cash returns featuring in the mix, or it is a bit early to think about that? Thank you.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Pieter, why don't you take both of those?

Pieter van der Does (Co-Founder and Co-CEO, Adyen): What I am excited about is we have large merchants, and we have a sophisticated account management team which has deep relationships with those merchants. To get a credit card number to Visa, that is not the most challenging thing you could do in the payments industry. It is everything around it. What I am really excited about is that we have the relationships with those merchants, which we develop over time, that they share with us what is needed, and that we can use that as a basis to further develop our strategy. That is also what you see what we have done this year with our acquisitions. That is what gives me the assurance that we are in a really good position. Capital allocation, let me give you the philosophical answer because I think that is what you are asking.
Currently, because it is a fraction of the number which has been flying around, it is just not so material and I think the company should focus on growth and only growth. But in theory, if this company would be a company that accumulates a lot of cash, then of course we should not be dogmatic about anything, and then it could be on the agenda. But now, consistent growth as we have delivered, like the last three half year reports, always 21%. That is the sort of boring numbers which we should bring forward.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Great. Thank you. The next question comes from Andrew Bauch from BMO. Andrew, please go ahead and unmute yourself and ask your question.

Andrew Bauch (Analyst, BMO): Hey, thanks for taking the question. Just want to take a step back and ask about the competitive landscape and what kind of differentiates today relative to recent history. Historically, authorization rates and ease of integration were the common talking points, but when you speak to merchants and prospective clients today, what are the primary aspects of the offering that would compel a decision to use Adyen or somebody else? With that lens, should we expect more regular tuck-ins like we've seen so far this year to address any potential competitive gaps?

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Do you want to take both of those, Pieter?

Pieter van der Does (Co-Founder and Co-CEO, Adyen): Yeah. I wish for the first one there was the golden bullet. It's different per merchant. For platforms, it can be mass onboarding and doing mass compliance, being able to onboard millions of sellers. Or it can be the fact that we do both online and have terminals. It can be our geographical spread. It can be moving away from legacy to single providers so just making things simpler. So it's really the breadth of our service that makes us win. Of course, auth rates is something which I think was really the card that we played in around 2011, and it will always be important. But we moved a little bit beyond that in the industry, and now other things are top of mind. Currently, what's top of mind is for merchants is "How are you going to help us through the Adyen Agentic threat for them?

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): In terms of M&A, should they expect more acquisitions going forward? Is M&A how we beat the competition?

Pieter van der Does (Co-Founder and Co-CEO, Adyen): No, because we have constantly developed new products. If you just hear me talking about the trends, most of those products, think financial service, Intelligent Money Movement, all those things we developed in-house. It is just that we always have for the core, we are always looking at building it ourselves. For adjacent, we always have looked internally and externally what is strategic to build yourself and what can you acquire. It just happened that it never happened, and that we always landed on internal. Now coincidentally, it happened twice in H1, but in the future, we still have an open mind to doing it, and it could be that we land internal and it could be differently, but we do not have a plan there to be an acquisition machine from now on.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Okay, great. The next question comes from Ramsey El-Assal from Cantor Fitzgerald. Ramsey, please go ahead and ask your question.

Ramsey El-Assal (Analyst, Cantor Fitzgerald): Hi. Thank you very much. Some of your competitors, very broadly defined, have built out branded consumer checkout wallets, I guess for a smoother checkout experience. I am thinking of like a Stripe Link or a Shop Pay. I know you are long-term oriented to focus on the merchant stack, but could a consumer dimension to your strategy kind of emerge at some point? Thank you.

Pieter van der Does (Co-Founder and Co-CEO, Adyen): Yeah, that's a great question. Currently, we are focusing pure on the merchant and are not doing that, and it's appreciated by our merchants because if you look which part of the market we operate, it's typically the large merchants which consider their shoppers their domain. For example, in the past if you look at why we want eBay. It's because eBay wanted to work with a partner that is only on the merchant side, and that is not signing up each consumer or seller also themselves. So you have different choices in this market, and that is great. This choice works well for us.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Great. Thank you for your question. The next question comes from Gus Galá from MCH. Please go ahead and unmute yourself and ask your question.

Gus Galá (Analyst, MCH): Hi, Pieter. Hi. Thank you for taking my questions. Following up on the wallet share ramp curve, I was curious could you talk a little bit about what you're seeing those ramps look like across the pillars, maybe deltas across those? Then as we think about Talon.One and Orb, how should we think about potentially that changing the wallet share ramps as you fold in those acquisitions? Lastly, just tying it all together. I mean, the revenue model is shifting more and more towards the pre- and post-auth over time. It'll become a greater portion of the value we'll offer, right? As we think of for instance, the pre-authorization transaction. Is this going to be more comprised of a platform subscription fee, a revenue share on incremental conversion? Just help us think about that. Thank you.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Great. Thanks. Hwa, you want to take that first one, Pieter, the second one?

Hwa Tsao (Interim CFO, Adyen): Yeah. Share of wallet ramp tends to be similar actually across pillars, but platforms are typically, they do take a little bit longer to ramp, just given their own go-to-market motions and the fact that, as Pieter mentioned. Sometimes they have many, many sub-merchants as we go forward.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Great. Pieter?

Pieter van der Does (Co-Founder and Co-CEO, Adyen): On the second one, we look at adding value for merchants, and we price for that. That means that look, we have large deals, and those deals have sophisticated pricing, and that can be priced over different elements. And that is what we do.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): All right. The next question comes from Craig Maurer, from FT Partners. Craig, please go ahead and ask your question.

Craig Maurer (Analyst, FT Partners): Yeah, thank you. I wanted to return to the OpenAI discussion for a moment. I just think it is important to understand whether you won their usage-based billing versus just their plain vanilla credit card payments, so whether you won their enterprise business or more their general subscription business. So we understand if this is still an opportunity to go after with Orb. Secondly, platform take rate was somewhat weaker than we had been expecting, so any context there would be helpful. Thanks.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Pieter, do you want to take that first one and Hwa, the second one?

Pieter van der Does (Co-Founder and Co-CEO, Adyen): On the OpenAI, it is their payment. It is the payments which their clients pay to them, and no forward-looking statements on that.

Hwa Tsao (Interim CFO, Adyen): Yeah, on the platform take rates, I think that the way to think about it is platforms tend to be larger customers. As we mentioned, our customers work on, we gain share of wallet with them, we grow with them, and we incentivize them to bring even more volume to our platform through the tiered pricing model. So it is a natural result of platform scaling with us.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Great. Thank you. We have time for one last question, and it's going to be with Nooshin, from Deutsche Bank. Nooshin, please go ahead and unmute yourself and ask your question.

Nooshin Nejati (Analyst, Deutsche Bank): Hi. Thanks for squeezing me in. I just have also a follow-up on OpenAI, and I appreciate you can't discuss customer specifics, but when you are thinking about the bigger opportunities ahead and how you can expand your partnership and thinking about Orb, I'm just wondering, do you believe the platform is already capable of supporting businesses operating at OpenAI's scale, or is there still meaningful investment required before it can address the most demanding enterprise use cases? So I'm specifically asking about Orb and if it needs more investment in there. And when it comes to Adyen Agentic is this also part of OpenAI relationship or what you're thinking about in the future? Thank you.

Pieter van der Does (Co-Founder and Co-CEO, Adyen): What I think is that if the largest companies are very sophisticated in who they partner with and that they partner for payments with us, it's a trend that we have seen over the years and which is continuing, and that's how I also look at that relationship. The reason to work with Orb is that we can onboard AI native companies. So that is separate from that. What you see is that the AI native companies grow very fast, and the billing sits in their infrastructure. So where we take that, you'll see that in the future. Did I answer all questions?

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Just a little bit on Agentic. Are we working with Agentic.

Pieter van der Does (Co-Founder and Co-CEO, Adyen): On Agentic, yes. You have to look at Agentic as comparable to payment methods that we can route a transaction to the different payment methods as needed. This is with Agentic. Companies, if you have something on stock, you want to be able to publish it on Agentic, then you want to be able to publish it on multiple Agentic protocols. You could theoretically, as a merchant, connect to all those different protocols because remember, there's no standardization. So you could implement to all those different protocols, or you could work with one supplier, Adyen. In order to get the transaction back to you would have to implement all of that. Or you could again, work with Adyen, that's what we do with Agentic.
What is important for us and philosophically, we want merchant choice and we want to be agnostic, that's what we do now that's also what you see back when we talk about later, we'll talk about machine to machine. You'll see the same elements always coming back because that's philosophically close to us.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Great. With that, we are out of time. Thank you all so much for joining us today. Have a great day.

Maggie O'Donnell (Investor Relations Representative, Adyen): Hello everyone, and thank you for joining Adyen's H1 2026 earnings call. My name is Maggie O'Donnell from Investor Relations, and I will be hosting today's call. With me today are Pieter, our co-founder and co-CEO, and Hwa, our incoming Interim CFO. We are going to begin with playing the prepared remarks from Ingo and Hwa, then Pieter will say a few words, and finally, we will open it up for Q&A with Pieter and Hwa. If you would like to ask a question, please use the raise hand functionality at the bottom of your screen. With that, let us get started.

Ingo Uytdehaage (Co-CEO, Adyen): Hello, everyone. The beginning of 2026 was a strategically important half for Adyen. As commerce rapidly evolves, we are enabling more of the world's largest merchants to capture greater value across the entire commerce journey. We grow faster than our market. This consistent outperformance is driven by two engines. First, we are winning new and diverse customers. Second, we are deepening relationships and expanding our share of wallet with existing ones. Both reflect our ability to continuously deliver new value for our customers. Our long-term relationships provide clear visibility into the durability of this growth. Merchants typically expand their share of wallet with Adyen from under 20% in years three to seven, to more than 40% after year 12. Even after more than a decade, customers like Uber, Microsoft, Spotify, and Google continue to broaden their use of our platform.
This sustained expansion gives us ultimate confidence in our resilience and ability to continue outperforming the market. The strong momentum reflected in our H1 performance comes from our unchanged mission, solving complexity for our merchants. The complexity is only increasing as commerce rapidly evolves. Competition for consumer attention is fiercer than ever. Workflows are shifting rapidly to AI, and legacy infrastructure is no longer sufficient to meet the demands of modern digital commerce. Our long-term strategy is built for exactly this shift, which is why more customers are looking to us as a stronger partner. Our North Star is to become the single trusted platform for the financial infrastructure on which global commerce runs. We started by building the world's most advanced payments processing stack. Now we are expanding that same engineering first mindset to solve customer pain points before at and after the transaction.
Our payments engine remains our foundation, and it continues to win share, but we are no longer just a payments company. We are the complete financial operating system for modern commerce, from payments to loyalty, billing, and Intelligent Money Movement. You can see this focus in high impact milestones we delivered this half. First, we completed the acquisitions of Talon.One and Orb, moving us deeper into our customers' technology stack and extending our platform well beyond payments. Talon.One brings market-leading promotions and loyalty capabilities into our single platform. Combined with our unique online and in-person transaction data, it allows merchants to finally deliver truly omnichannel loyalty at scale. For years, retailers have struggled to connect digital and physical customer experiences.
By bringing loyalty natively into our architecture, merchants can recognize shoppers across channels and deliver personalized incentives in real time, deepening consumer engagement and making loyalty far more effective than standalone systems ever could. Orb addresses another growing customer challenge. As AI transforms how software is built and consumed, usage-based billing is becoming the default pricing model for many businesses. Orb gives merchants the tools to automate metering, pricing, and billing, while our payment infrastructure completes the revenue life cycle by connecting usage directly to settlement. Together, this gives businesses a single system to launch flexible pricing models globally and at scale. These acquisitions are an important part of our long-term strategy, serving as powerful drivers of our growth. They represent our fundamental long-term belief that in a complex world, the company that facilitates revenue optimization will deliver the most value.
It also reflects how we invest, selectively, with discipline, and where we see clear strategic logic. Second, we introduced Adyen Agentic to solve a critical problem for our merchants, how to sell safely and efficiently in the emerging AI agent economy. Without a universal standard, merchants would need to build and maintain dozens of separate integrations just to keep their inventory, pricing, and payments in sync. This creates massive operational cost and risk. Our product suite solves this. It acts as the universal translator that allows merchants to connect once to our platform and securely accept payments across all major Agentic protocols, all while using the same unified fraud detection and compliance rules they trust today. Third, we officially launched Intelligent Money Movement. For large enterprise merchants, complexity doesn't end at a point of payment — i t often begins there.
We help businesses automate global money movement on a single unified platform. Because this occurs natively on our own technical and banking infrastructure, capital flows dynamically and without the frictional delays of traditional banking rails. It allows us to move money completely end to end, unlocking unprecedented speed and treasury efficiency, so global businesses can simplify their most complex operations. Taken together, these capabilities make Adyen a more strategic partner to our customers and strengthen our long-term growth opportunity. The success of this strategy is directly reflected in our financial results this half. We delivered a strong half of 2026, with net revenue up 21% on a constant currency basis, driven by this ongoing platform expansion. Our scale is already immense. We are processing billions of transactions for thousands of global merchants. In the first half alone, we processed EUR 804 billion in volume.
To reiterate, we are winning in the market because we are building the complete financial operating system for modern commerce. As we look to the second half of 2026 and beyond, we will continue to execute with the same speed, discipline, and engineering-first mindset that has brought us here. We hold ourselves to the same standard with you, our shareholders, setting clear commitments and delivering against them consistently. To speak more to our operation execution and financial performance, I'll now hand things over to our interim CFO, Hwa Tsao. Hwa, over to you.

Hwa Tsao (Interim CFO, Adyen): Hello, everyone. I am Hwa Tsao, Adyen's incoming interim CFO. For the past year, I have worked alongside the management board as the SVP of Group Finance, and I am thrilled to step into this role at such a strategically important time for Adyen, marked by our recent acquisitions of Talon.One and Orb, the launch of Intelligent Money Movement and Adyen Agentic, and so much more. My focus is on empowering our incredible team to serve our customers and continuing our history of financial discipline while keeping our dialogue with our investors transparent and constructive. Now, let us turn to our financials, beginning with our top-line results. Net revenue was EUR 1.3 billion in the first half, up 19% year-over-year or 21% on a constant currency basis, with continued strong growth in line with our communicated guidance. The best way to understand Adyen's net revenue growth is through our building blocks.
First, expanding share of wallet with existing customers. Second, ramping up previous year cohorts. Third, winning new merchants, and fourth, scaling our financial products. We drove roughly two-thirds of our growth by deepening relationships with our existing merchants, specifically those onboarded before 2025. As Ingo highlighted, compounding revenue from established merchant cohorts is a valuable driver of our business. When our merchants expand, we grow with them. In addition, as we help them solve more challenges across products and geographies, we increase our share of their wallet. These levers, combined with volume-based tiered pricing, incentivize our merchants to consolidate more of their business onto our platform as they scale. The remainder of our growth came from the ramp of our 2025 cohort, new customer wins in 2026, and the expansion of our financial products offering.
These levers lay the foundation for the future as more recent wins scale and drive our continued growth for years to come. To support this expanding business, we added 249 net new joiners in the first half, bringing our total FTEs to 5,020 at the end of June. Our disciplined and targeted approach to hiring focused primarily on technical and go-to-market roles to drive our product roadmap and commercial momentum. With this focus, we remain well on track for our full-year goal of 550 to 650 net new hires. This measured pace of investment directly supported our strong profitability. EBITDA reached EUR 642 million for the first half, up 18% year-over-year for an EBITDA margin of 49%. Excluding one-time transaction costs, EBITDA margin landed at 50%, in line with H1 2025 and our previously communicated expectations.
CapEx was EUR 64 million or 5% of net revenue in the first half. The majority of our CapEx is related to data centers. Our core infrastructure operates on our own private cloud, which creates a commercial advantage and allows us to deliver operational efficiency as we scale. Historically, most of the value in payments sat at a point of authorization, improving acceptance rates, optimizing routing, and managing cost. Before a payment is made, our customers are making increasingly complex decisions around which transactions to allow through, how to balance conversion and risk, and how to shape the outcome.
